subject: maths
title: Numbers to 20
introductionText:
Term 1 · Number
Numbers to 20
The Big Idea: A number tells us how many. When we count, we touch each thing once,
and the last number we say is how many there are altogether.
Say It Like This
Read aloud
"Numbers are names for how many. When we count, we touch each thing once and say
one number for it: one, two, three... The last number we say tells us how many there are.
Look — if I spread the spoons out, are there more now? No! Moving things doesn't make
more. We still have the same number."
Watch Out For
The slip almost every child makes
1. Saying numbers faster than touching. His mouth runs ahead of his finger, so he skips
an object or counts one twice. Slow him down: "Push each spoon to the side as you count
it." Moved objects can't be counted again.
2. Thinking spread-out means more. A long line of 6 looks like "more" than a tight pile of
6. Let him count both and discover they match.
3. Writing teen numbers backwards. We say "four-teen" — the four comes first — but
we write 14 with the 1 first. Say it this way: "Fourteen is ten and four. The ten is written
first."
Try It at Home
Game 1 — The spoon trick (5 minutes)
Put 7 spoons in a tight row. Count them together, sliding each one as you count. Now
spread them all over the table and ask: "How many are there now?" Let him guess before
counting. Most six-year-olds want to count again — that's fine. The day he says "still 7, I
didn't take any away" without counting, the idea has landed.
Game 2 — Flash the dice (3 minutes)
Roll one dice, show it for two seconds, then hide it. "How many dots?" Children can learn
to see up to 6 dots at a glance without counting one by one. Then use two dice. Can he
see 5 and 3 and know it is 8?
Counted in a row:
1 2 3 4 5
3
1
Spread out:
5
2
4
Still 5 apples!
Count the top row with him, touching each apple. Then ask how many are in the bottom row before he
counts — the answer is the same.
More examples to talk about
• An egg box holds 10 or 12 eggs. Count the empty holes too.
• Things you can't touch can still be counted: claps, jumps, the ding of a spoon on a glass.
Close his eyes and ask him to count the claps.
• Tricky: the number on a bus or a house door is a name, not a count. Bus 13 doesn't have
13 passengers.
• Tricky: if you count the same toys starting from a different one, you still get the same
answer.
• Twenty is two tens — the fingers of two people's hands.
Key Words
count number how many altogether the same more digit

True or false? Sara counted 6 cups in a row. Then she spread them out. Now there are
more than 6 cups.
sourceQuestions.answerKeyText: False. There are still 6 cups — moving them doesn't make more.

sourceQuestions.sourceText: Count something in your room. What did you count, and how many were there?
sourceQuestions.answerKeyText: Any real object and a correct count, e.g. "I counted my cars, there were 9."

The last number you say when you count tells you...
( which is the biggest ) ( which is the first one ) ( how many altogether )

How many dots fill a whole ten frame?
( 10 ) ( 20 ) ( 5 )

5 spoons were in a pile. Now they are in a long line. How many spoons are there?
( more than 5 ) ( fewer than 5 ) ( 5 )
